steps.html:
Shift 1 of 5

Meet every student

Slow thinking· for students

Now
In one grade, students’ levels vary widely. Software that taught each student at their own level raised math scores 0.36 SD in 4.5 months (Delhi, 2019). One study; mixed elsewhere.
Next
Every student starts on their own rung: catching up from below, racing ahead from above, checked as they go — and the teacher told who’s slipping.

Unguarded GPT-4: practice up 48%, exam scores down 17% once it was removed. A guarded tutor didn’t do that harm (PNAS 2025).

The school gives every student a flexible tutor that asks before it tells. Because the school owns it, the teacher sees how each student uses it and thinks.

steps.title: Understanding is the only thing left worth grading
steps.html:
How we break the habit

When the answer is free, understanding is the only thing left worth grading.

Goodhart’s law bites hardest on one narrow, high-stakes number.
1
Measure the thing itself.
The reasoning, not a stand-in for it.
2
Many small looks, not one big test.
Low stakes, so nothing is worth gaming.
3
A person reads it.
Judgment, not just a score.
Honestly
State tests and the MCAT aren’t going away soon. If understanding is what we look at every day, the test becomes a by-product.

steps.title: It can go wrong, sometimes quietly
steps.html:
Honest about the risks

It can go wrong, sometimes quietly.

1
Free tools help the already-engaged most. Devices and broadband aren’t equal.
2
Over-reliance, for students and for us: if we trust the summary, our own judgment gets weaker.
3
A rung can harden into a label. Placement has to stay fluid.
4
AI is wrong sometimes: a summary said a student had done nothing; an exam question can be ambiguous.
5
A record of how a child thinks is sensitive: who owns it, how long it’s kept, breaches.
6
Goodhart applies to AI too: optimize engagement or scores, and it bends the same way.
7
One 2026 trial (not peer-reviewed): a course AI tutor lowered grades, most for first-generation students.
The rule
AI reads. You decide.

steps.title: What I’d ask of any AI in a classroom
steps.html:
Where I land
Fast tools for us. Slow thinking for them.

What I’d ask of any AI in a classroom

1
The student tries first.
It never gives the answer before they commit.
2
The teacher sees every exchange.
3
It meets each student at their level.
And tells the teacher who is falling behind.
4
It looks at reasoning.
And gives second chances.
5
Everything it makes is checked.
Mistakes are fixed in public.
We can do better.
My hope is that this is an enabling technology.
